original_passages.text: This section distinguishes three response laws: a sharp threshold with exact inactivity below it, the original tanh approximation with a signed response below threshold, and an optional smooth law with exact inactivity. Smoothness of a scalar switch and smoothness of its composition with a gradient magnitude are separate questions. None establishes a solution to the Clay Mathematics Institute Navier–Stokes problem.
Velocity field, time, and spatial gradient in a specified continuous domain.
Pressure divided by constant density; distinct from the actor set P elsewhere.
Kinematic viscosity in the chosen analogy.
Response-strength and density parameters; σ a(q)/ρ has acceleration units.
Modeled field; its regularity and coupling need specifying.
Euclidean gradient magnitude; not differentiable as a function of the gradient at zero.
Threshold in gradient units; τ₀/η is an optional dimensionally compatible calibration.
Response transition scale, with the same units as q.
Gradient regularization scale in gδ; same units as the gradient. Distinct from a Dirac delta.
Sharp exact-off, original signed tanh, and optional smooth exact-off response laws.
Fixed unit direction; no automatic claim of opposition to motion.

Choose the response law a before using the equation. Sharp threshold: a₀(q) = max(q, 0), so the added force is zero for q ≤ 0 and proportional to q for q > 0. This law is continuous but not differentiable at q = 0.

Original tanh choice: aₜ(q) = q[1 + tanh(q/ε)]/2, with ε > 0. It is smooth as a function of q, but for finite q < 0 it is negative and nonzero. For example, aₜ(−ε) ≈ −0.119203ε. The force therefore reverses direction below threshold when σ > 0; it does not simply switch off. A small tail may be intentional, but its sign and interpretation must be stated.

Zero-gradient concern: |v| is not differentiable at v = 0. Composing it with tanh does not automatically remove that issue; a particular composition can have cancellations, which need checking. For a smooth alternative, use gδ(v) = √(v · v + δ²) − δ with δ > 0, and qδ = gδ(∇S) − Γcrit. This changes the gradient measure near zero and is a modeling choice.

Optional smooth exact-off response: aε(q) = 0 for q ≤ 0, and aε(q) = q exp[−(ε/q)²] for q > 0. For fixed ε > 0 this scalar function is C∞, including the join at zero. Using aε(qδ) with fixed δ > 0 makes the constitutive response smooth in the gradient variable and exactly zero when qδ ≤ 0. This is an alternative to the tanh law, not a property of it. Its positive onset in the original magnitude is |∇S| > √(Γcrit² + 2δΓcrit), so the threshold must be calibrated in the chosen measure. To retain the original cutoff |∇S| = Γcrit instead, use the calibrated excess qδ* = √(|∇S|² + δ²) − √(Γcrit² + δ²). It has the same sign as |∇S| − Γcrit for Γcrit ≥ 0. Using aε(qδ*) gives a smooth exact-off alternative with that original cutoff; the response above it is still a changed constitutive law.

A fixed eₖ specifies direction; it does not guarantee drag or energy dissipation. For f to remove kinetic energy pointwise, u · f must be nonpositive. The model still needs a domain, initial and boundary data, a definition or equation for S, and compatible coefficient units. A smooth constitutive response is not a proof of smooth solutions for all time. Pressure, viscosity, yield, and boundary remain modeling language unless independently operationalized.

Tracks a paired rescaling of two scalar variables. For λ > 0, scaling S by λ and R by 1/λ preserves their product. This is an algebraic invariance under a specified transformation; no equilibrium or time conservation follows without a dynamical model. The precise description is a product preserved under reciprocal scaling. This transformation property does not establish stability or boundedness of a subsequent time evolution.
Two-component vector of scalar variables for this model; distinct from spatial x elsewhere.
Paired scaling factor; division requires nonzero λ, and positivity preserves signs.
Scalar environmental-context variable in this static model.
Product invariant under the stated reciprocal rescaling; not an established dynamic equilibrium.

Treats status or context as a signed field over a specified spatial embedding. Advection carries the field, diffusion spreads it, and a localized source changes it. A network alone does not specify the continuous geometry needed for these derivatives. With constant D_diff ≥ 0 and ∇ · u = 0, the following transport form is also a conservative continuity form.
A(t) = ∫₀ᵗ γ[U(s) − Ubaseline] ds,     J(t) = κ A(t).

Kₕ is a smooth localized kernel of width h > 0 with spatial integral 1. The original δ(x − x₀) is an alternative point-source idealization interpreted as a distribution, not an ordinary smooth function. A stores accumulated input; κ converts that stored quantity to a source rate with the required units. This retains the original memory choice explicitly. Under closed or periodic boundaries, constant positive excess utility can make the total field grow quadratically in time because the stored input is integrated again by the evolution equation. If instantaneous production is intended instead, specify J(t) = γ[U(t) − Ubaseline] with suitable units; that is a different model. Negative excess input may lower this signed field. Initial and boundary data remain necessary. For compressible transport, replace u · ∇S by ∇ · (Su).
Signed status or context field over a specified continuous spatial embedding.
Advection velocity; divergence-free for the displayed conservative interpretation.
Constant diffusion coefficient, with units length²/time.

The sharp version defines exactly what happens on both sides: the additional boundary force is zero at and below threshold, and active above it. Zero added force does not mean the whole system is stable; the other terms still evolve. The smooth alternatives and their distinct behavior are specified in the earlier threshold section.

T is the symmetric viscous stress for the stated incompressible Newtonian analogy. The earlier µ₀∇u was a scaled velocity-gradient tensor, not this full stress. This constitutive choice does not establish literal fluid behavior in a social system.
Γcrit ≥ 0. Optional calibration: Γcrit = τ₀/η, with τ₀ ≥ 0 and η > 0.
q = |∇S| − Γcrit;     a₀(q) = 0 if q ≤ 0, and a₀(q) = q if q > 0.

Assume constant ρ > 0, µ > 0, and σ ≥ 0; p = P/ρ and ν = µ/ρ connect this equation to the earlier normalized form. The calibration η must give Γcrit the same units as |∇S|. Increasing η lowers Γcrit at fixed τ₀, so the label rigidity does not by itself establish stronger resistance. Fixed-direction forcing is not necessarily dissipative. Initial and boundary data, the S coupling, and a domain are required; smooth activation alone does not establish well-posedness or global regularity.

distinctions: The original A/S equations specify transport, source accumulation, activation and momentum; the checked passages do not specify a gravitational G.
Carrying continuity is preserved through changing configurations; it is not interpreted as a constant energy or frozen state.
The broader guard relationship leaves its response functions and physical stress as choices; it does not supply an A/S energy mapping.
The retained scalar product S*R in the reciprocal-scaling example is a static algebraic relation, not the identified dynamic spatial-field energy.
In the actual record implementation delta_E is a symmetric strain change. Material record energy is the already-accounted fabric energy, not another energy named delta_E.
Social retrieval depends on retained records and feeds utility/source selection, but these passages do not assign its own independent energy debit.
historical_review: The broader original-corpus and archived-board searches remain historical evidence. No new exhaustive search of all notes, chats, images, or live boards is claimed.
